transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-09
Time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sasha Kim (Redwood Solutions), Miguel Soto (Argon CTO), Anika Rao (Argon ML Eng), Liam Chen (Argon DevOps), Rina Patel (Argon Security)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, quick intro — i'm jordan from redwood, priya is our se who'll drive the tech bits.
[00:18] Miguel: hey thanks, excited. we've been looking at quantized inference to reduce costs, particularly for our embe— embedding and chat endpoints.
[00:30] Priya: great, so agenda today is run through int8 vs fp8 vs gptq and awq, show some microbenchmarks, and discuss accuracy regressions and on-prem implications, and then next steps.
[00:45] Anika: quick note — our baseline is a 13B decoder-only model (fork of open-arch) and we are seeing about 140ms p95 on hosted with fp16, but cost is high. we want to drop to <80ms p95 and cut token cost by ~3x if possible.
[01:05] Priya: okay sounds good, and what's your typical sequence length distribution?
[01:12] Liam: 80–350 tokens, 95th around 280; a lot of long conversations for our assistance product.
[01:20] Priya: important — longer sequences emphasize kv cache size and memory; some quant methods affect kv layout. we'll walk through that.

[01:40] Priya: first, quick definitions — INT8: symmetric/asymmetric quantization that targets weights to 8-bit. gives big memory and compute wins on GPU kernels that support int8 matmul. FP8: reduced floating point that keeps dynamic range, can help accuracy vs int8 but requires hardware support or emulation. GPTQ: offline per-channel quantization tuned to 4-bit/8-bit, often good for minimal accuracy loss but can be slow to generate. AWQ: advanced weight-only quant that aims to match fp16 accuracy while enabling int8-like speed.
[02:12] Miguel: can you give heuristics for accuracy regression risk across these?
[02:20] Priya: sure — generally FP8 > AWQ approx >= GPTQ > naive INT8 in accuracy (FP8 being closest to fp16), but it depends on model architecture and layerwise sensitivity. AWQ is promising because it tends to preserve quantization-sensitive layers with per-block compensation. GPTQ with 4-bit can be excellent but setup time and model fidelity testing is heavier.
[02:50] Sasha: i'll add that in our internal benchmarks awq had lower perplexity deltas on conversation sets vs int8, but int8 still gave highest TPS on T4-like instances.

[03:10] Anika: what about runtime differences — latency and throughput tradeoffs?
[03:18] Priya: int8 typically gives the largest raw speedups on inference—30–2x depending on kernel and hardware; on A100/H100 int8 kernels can saturate compute for token generation, but if kv cache bandwidth becomes bottleneck for long sequences, gains diminish. AWQ/GPTQ often get similar memory reductions but may rely on fallback emulation for some ops which hurts latency. FP8 on H100 is very fast if native kernel available.
[03:50] Miguel: so in our case with long sequences the kv cache could become the limiting factor — are there optimizations?
[03:58] Priya: yes — continuous KV caching reduces recomputation, and our runtime uses tiled KV packing to improve memory locality. for quantized weights, we keep kv in fp16 or bf16 to avoid precision loss in attention accumulation — recommended for long contexts. that means you might not see full memory wins on kv but you still get weight memory reduction.
[04:25] Liam: so we'd still keep kv cache in fp16 even if weights are int8?
[04:30] Priya: correct, typical production pattern: weights quantized, activations and kv kept in fp16/bfp16 for stability. it's a tradeoff but preserves accuracy for long seqs.

[04:50] Miguel: what about batching? we need decent throughput for multi-user QPS spikes, but can't inflate latency.
[04:58] Priya: redwood runtime supports dynamic batching and continuous batching. for quantized kernels batching usually increases amortized cost per token—higher throughput but latency SLO depends on queueing. Another lever is batching windows — we recommend short windows (5–30ms) for low-latency apps; for throughput-heavy backgrounds you can allow larger windows. quantization does not change the batching behavior much but it changes the sweet spot since kernels are faster.

[05:30] Anika: any gotchas with model variants — like we use a small adapter and prompt-tuning?
[05:38] Priya: adapters and LoRA usually quantize fine but require re-quant or special handling for low-bit methods; AWQ tends to preserve adapters better. GPTQ sometimes requires re-quant on the adapter layer. we should test your actual fork.

[06:00] Sasha: pulling up benchmark slide — (link: https://redwood.ai/decks/quant-bench-2027) — okay slide shows p50/p95 for 13B on H100 with int8, AWQ and fp8. numbers are illustrative: int8 p95 = 55ms, AWQ p95 = 72ms, FP8 p95 = 60ms, baseline fp16 p95 = 140ms. throughput (tokens/sec) int8 highest, AWQ slightly lower.
[06:40] Miguel: those look great for latency but what about accuracy on our eval set?
[06:45] Priya: we've run our convo eval set — int8 had 3.9% drop in accuracy on our QA metric, AWQ 0.8% drop, FP8 0.6% (near-zero). GPTQ 4-bit had 1.2% drop but preserved some areas better. caveat — that's on off-the-shelf model; forks can shift sensitivity.

[07:15] Rina: security question — if we deploy on-prem or VPC, can we use AWQ and still keep key material inside our KMS?
[07:22] Jordan: yes — private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM; inference kernels run in your VPC and key unwrap occurs inside your control plane. logs and traces can be disabled or sanitized. we'll share SOC2 and KMS integration docs.

[07:40] Liam: ops — what's the effort to test and roll a quantized variant? can we do canary on dedicated pool?
[07:48] Priya: yes — typical flow: generate quantized model artifacts (we can do int8, awq, or gptq), run offline eval and regression tests (perplexity, precision/recall on your test suite), then do canary on dedicated pool with traffic split and automatic rollback on metric regression. Redwood console supports per-route rollout controls.

[08:15] Anika: about regression detection — what metrics should we watch?
[08:20] Priya: tokens per request, latency p50/p95, perplexity on heldout, custom QA accuracy, and embedding drift (cosine delta). we have automated eval hooks that can run your prompt set against baseline and quant variant.

[08:45] Miguel: you mentioned KV caching kept in fp16 — doesn't that limit memory reductions for int8?
[08:50] Priya: yes to an extent; weight storage is reduced significantly but kv consumes a large portion for long sequences. For example, for 13B at 280 tokens, kv might be ~40% of activation memory. If you need more reduction, mixed strategies like per-layer activation quantization or offloading older kv to host memory are options but increase latency.

[09:18] Sasha: also note GPU selection matters — T4/RTX class supports int8 well with TensorRT, H100 has FP8 native and faster mixed-precision int8; choice impacts both throughput and accuracy tradeoff.

[09:35] Miguel: oh — we plan to run dedicated on-prem racks with A100s; do you have guidance?
[09:42] Priya: A100's int8 support exists but H100's FP8 gives better fp16 parity. For A100, AWQ and GPTQ often give the best balance: they preserve accuracy with good speedups though raw int8 might beat them. We'll provide microbenchmarks specifically on A100.

[10:05] Liam: what's the size impact — how much smaller are model files with AWQ vs int8?
[10:12] Priya: AWQ typically compresses weights to ~30–40% of fp16 size depending on block sizes; int8 around 50% if symmetric per-tensor, GPTQ 25–33% for 4-bit. FP8 is around 50% of fp16 depending on implementation.

[10:35] Anika: run-of-the-mill question: inference stability — do we see hallucination or behavior changes with quantized models?
[10:42] Priya: sometimes, particularly with low-bit quant (4-bit GPTQ) you can get more generation drift on open-ended tasks; for classification or retrieval-augmented generation it's less risky. That's why we recommend prompt-set regression tests. AWQ tends to minimize behavioral drift.

[11:05] Jordan: sharing a link in chat to the benchmark spreadsheet — https://redwood.ai/bench/argon-13b-int8-awq (placeholder). we'll add columns for your eval metrics.

[11:20] Miguel: operational question — if we need to fall back from a quantized variant to fp16 under load, can routing take care of that?
[11:27] Priya: yes — smart routing supports model variant fallback by policy — e.g., prefer AWQ, fallback to fp16 if SLOs violated or if quantized pool capacity exhausted. This is seamless at API level.

[11:45] Rina: compliance — will audit logs show model artifacts and quant config?
[11:50] Jordan: yes, we log model version, quantization profile, kernel config and rollout decisions. With Private you can retain logs in your SIEM; console shows token-level traces with sampling controls.

[12:10] Anika: can we test AWQ on our fork without full GPTQ pipeline?
[12:16] Priya: yes — AWQ is weight-only and has a lighter conversion pipeline; we can prepare a conversion and share artifacts. GPTQ needs a heavier offline pass and it's longer.

[12:35] Liam: we have throughput spikes — can autoscaling react to quantized pools?
[12:40] Priya: yes — dedicated pools autoscale; quantized pools are just model variants on GPUs. Autoscaling rules can be capacity or latency-driven. For very spiky loads we recommend reserved baseline capacity plus autoscale bursts.

[13:05] Miguel: ok let's talk timeline and pilot scope — we want a pilot within 3 weeks if possible.
[13:12] Jordan: sounds feasible: week 1 conversion+offline eval, week 2 canary on dedicated with small traffic, week 3 ramp and regression review.

[13:30] Priya: action items recap — we'll run A100 microbenchmarks for your fork, run KV-enabled tests, and prepare conversion artifacts for AWQ and INT8. Jordan will send pricing, and security will send KMS/SOC2 docs.

[13:50] Miguel: perfect, thanks everyone.
[14:00] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule the pilot kickoff.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcription contains minor mislabels and filler; references to links were shared in chat.
